rows.stem: Define rate of reaction. Write two factors that affect the rate of reaction.
rows.solution:
The RATE OF REACTION is the change in the concentration of a reactant or a product per unit time — the DECREASE in the concentration of a reactant, or the INCREASE in the concentration of a product:
\(\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{\Delta[\text{Reactant}]}{\Delta t} = +\dfrac{\Delta[\text{Product}]}{\Delta t}\)

The MINUS sign for the reactant is not cosmetic. Its concentration falls, so \(\Delta[\mathrm{R}]\) is negative, and the sign makes the rate come out positive as a rate must.

Its usual units are \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).

TWO FACTORS THAT AFFECT IT, any two of the following.

CONCENTRATION of the reactants — more molecules per unit volume means more collisions per second, so the rate rises. How steeply is what the ORDER of the reaction measures.

TEMPERATURE — raising it increases both the number of collisions and, far more importantly, the FRACTION of them energetic enough to cross the activation barrier. A rise of ten degrees near room temperature roughly doubles the rate.

A CATALYST lowers the activation energy by offering a different path; SURFACE AREA matters for a solid reactant, and the NATURE of the reactants themselves sets the barrier in the first place.

rows.stem:
Arrange the following compounds as directed : (any Two)
(i) In decreasing order of basic strength in aqueous solution :
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\), \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_3N}\)
(ii) In increasing order of solubility in water :
\(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\)
(iii) In decreasing order of their pKb values :
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{NH_3}\)
rows.solution:
(i) DECREASING order of basic strength in AQUEOUS solution:
\(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH} > (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_3\mathrm{N} > \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\)

Two effects compete in water and neither wins outright. Each ethyl group RELEASES electron density and makes the lone pair more available, which favours the tertiary amine. But the conjugate acid must be stabilised by HYDROGEN BONDING to water, which needs hydrogens on the nitrogen — three for the primary amine's cation, two for the secondary, only one for the tertiary — and the three bulky ethyl groups also obstruct a proton's approach. The SECONDARY amine, sharing in both advantages, comes out strongest.

(ii) INCREASING order of solubility in water:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} < (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NH} < \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\)

Solubility depends on hydrogen bonding to water, and falls as the hydrocarbon portion grows. Aniline's large benzene ring makes it only sparingly soluble; the secondary amine carries two ethyl groups and one \(\mathrm{N-H}\); the primary amine carries one ethyl group and TWO \(\mathrm{N-H}\) hydrogens, so it is the most soluble of the three.

(iii) DECREASING order of \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) values:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} > \mathrm{NH_3} > \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\)

A HIGHER \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a WEAKER base, so this order runs from weakest to strongest. Aniline is much the weakest, its lone pair delocalised into the ring and so unavailable. Ethylamine is the strongest, its ethyl group pushing density onto the nitrogen. Ammonia, with neither advantage nor disadvantage, sits between them.

rows.stem:
Write the Nernst equation for the following cell reaction :
\(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cu^{2+}\,(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}\,(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)
How will the \(\mathrm{E_{cell}}\) be affected when concentration of
(i) \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ions is increased and
(ii) \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) ions is increased ?
rows.solution:
The cell reaction transfers TWO electrons, and the solids do not enter the quotient:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]}\)

(i) Increasing \([\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]\): \(E_{\text{cell}}\) INCREASES.

The copper ion is in the DENOMINATOR, so raising it makes the fraction smaller, the logarithm more negative, and the quantity subtracted therefore negative — which adds to the standard value.

(ii) Increasing \([\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]\): \(E_{\text{cell}}\) DECREASES.

The zinc ion is in the NUMERATOR, so raising it makes the fraction larger, the logarithm positive, and a positive quantity is subtracted.

Le Chatelier's principle gives the same answers without any algebra. Copper(II) is a REACTANT, so adding it pushes the reaction forward and the cell works harder; zinc(II) is a PRODUCT, so adding it opposes the reaction. Checking the Nernst equation against this reasoning catches a sign error at once.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Following ions of 3d-transition series are given :
\(\mathrm{Ti^{4+}}\), \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\)
(Atomic number : Ti = 22, V = 23, Cr = 24, Mn = 25)
Identify the ion which is
(i) most stable in aqueous solution.
(ii) a strong oxidising agent.
(iii) colourless in aqueous solution.
Give suitable reason in each.
rows.solution:
Work out each configuration first. A transition metal loses its \(4s\) electrons before any \(3d\):
\(\mathrm{Ti^{4+}} = 3d^0\), \(\mathrm{V^{3+}} = 3d^2\), \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} = 3d^3\), \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}} = 3d^4\)

(i) MOST STABLE in aqueous solution: \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\).

Its three d electrons occupy the three lower orbitals of an octahedral field singly, giving a HALF-FILLED \(t_{2g}^3\) set. That arrangement is unusually stable — the electrons are spread as widely as possible and their spins are parallel — which is why \(+3\) is the characteristic state of chromium.

(ii) STRONG OXIDISING AGENT: \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\).

An oxidising agent is a species eager to GAIN an electron. Manganese(III) is \(3d^4\), and taking one electron gives \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), which is \(3d^5\) — an exactly half-filled d subshell and the most stable arrangement available. So manganese(III) is strongly inclined to be reduced.

(iii) COLOURLESS in aqueous solution: \(\mathrm{Ti^{4+}}\).

Colour in these ions arises from a D-D TRANSITION, an electron absorbing visible light and jumping from the lower set of d orbitals to the upper. Titanium(IV) is \(3d^0\) — it has NO d electrons at all, so no such jump is possible and its solutions are colourless. The other three all have electrons available and are coloured.

rows.stem:
(i) On the basis of crystal field theory, write the electronic configuration for \(\mathrm{d^4}\) ion if \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\).
(ii) Using valence bond theory, predict the hybridization and magnetic character of \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\).
(Atomic number of Ni = 28)
(iii) Write the formula of the following complex using IUPAC norms :
Dichloridobis (ethane-1,2-diamine) cobalt (III)
rows.solution:
(i) The configuration is \(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^1\).

An octahedral field splits the d orbitals into a lower set of three and an upper set of two, separated by \(\Delta_0\). Each electron chooses between promotion to the upper set, costing \(\Delta_0\), and pairing in the lower set, costing the pairing energy \(\mathrm{P}\).

With \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\) — a WEAK FIELD — promotion is the cheaper option, so the fourth electron goes UPSTAIRS rather than pairing. All four remain unpaired, giving a HIGH SPIN complex with \(\mu = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = 4{\cdot}90\) B.M.

(ii) Nickel is atomic number 28, so \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\). CYANIDE is a STRONG field ligand: it forces those eight electrons into FOUR of the five d orbitals as four pairs, which frees ONE inner \(3d\) orbital.

That orbital with the \(4s\) and two \(4p\) gives \(dsp^2\) hybridisation and a SQUARE PLANAR shape. Every electron is paired, so the complex is DIAMAGNETIC.

HYBRIDISATION: \(dsp^2\). MAGNETIC CHARACTER: diamagnetic.

(iii) The two chlorido ligands give \(-2\) and the two ethane-1,2-diamine ligands are neutral, so against cobalt's \(+3\) the complex ion carries \(+1\):
\(\mathrm{[CoCl_2(en)_2]^+}\)

The charge is not stated in the name, so it must be worked out from the oxidation state given in the bracket.

rows.stem:
When a co-ordination compound \(\mathrm{NiCl_2 \cdot 6H_2O}\) mixed with \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\), 2 moles of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) are precipitated per mole of the compound. Write
(i) Structural formula of the complex.
(ii) Secondary valency of 'Ni' in the complex.
(iii) IUPAC name of the complex.
rows.solution:
Two moles of silver chloride per mole of compound means TWO chlorides are FREE in solution, outside the coordination sphere. Neither is therefore a ligand, and the six water molecules must fill all six coordination positions.

(i) STRUCTURAL FORMULA: \(\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_6]Cl_2}\)

(ii) SECONDARY VALENCY: 6.

Werner's secondary valency is the COORDINATION NUMBER, the count of donor atoms bonded directly to the metal. Six water molecules, each monodentate, give six, and the geometry is octahedral. The PRIMARY valency is 2, matching nickel's \(+2\) state and the two chlorides outside.

(iii) IUPAC NAME: HEXAAQUANICKEL(II) CHLORIDE.

The complex is the cation, so it takes no \(-\mathrm{ate}\) suffix, and the counter ion is named last as a separate word.

Note that the precipitate test is exactly how Werner established such structures: the number of moles of silver chloride counts the chlorides OUTSIDE, and the rest of the formula must then be accounted for inside.

rows.stem:
A first order reaction is 50% complete in 40 minutes. Calculate the time required for the completion of 90% of reaction.
[Given : log 2 = 0.3010, log 10 = 1]
rows.solution:
The reaction is FIRST ORDER, so begin from the half-life. "50% complete in 40 minutes" IS the half-life:
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{k}\), giving \(k = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{40}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

If 90% has reacted, 10% REMAINS, so taking the initial amount as 100 the amount left is 10:
\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303 \times 40}{0{\cdot}693}\log\dfrac{100}{10}\)

Since \(\log 10 = 1\),
\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303 \times 40}{0{\cdot}693}\)

\(t = 132{\cdot}9\ \mathrm{min}\)

A quicker route counts half-lives. Falling to a tenth takes \(\log 10 / \log 2 = 1/0{\cdot}3010 = 3{\cdot}32\) half-lives, and \(3{\cdot}32 \times 40 = 132{\cdot}9\) minutes. That the answer lies between three and four half-lives is the check: three would leave 12.5% and four 6.25%.

rows.stem:
Illustrate the following reactions giving suitable example in each case :
(i) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis.
(ii) Carbylamine reaction.
(iii) Hoffmann bromamide degradation reaction.
rows.solution:
(i) GABRIEL PHTHALIMIDE SYNTHESIS, in three steps:
\(\text{phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KOH}} \text{potassium phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{C_2H_5Br}} \text{N-ethylphthalimide} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} + \text{sodium phthalate}\)

Potassium hydroxide removes the imide's acidic \(\mathrm{N-H}\) hydrogen, made acidic by the two flanking carbonyls; the anion then displaces bromide in an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) step; alkaline hydrolysis frees the amine. Its value is that it gives a PURE PRIMARY amine, with no secondary or tertiary contamination. It fails for aromatic amines, an aryl halide not undergoing that substitution.

(ii) CARBYLAMINE REACTION — a test for PRIMARY amines, giving an isocyanide of exceptionally foul smell:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_2H_5NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Forming the isocyanide requires the nitrogen to give up BOTH of its hydrogens, so secondary and tertiary amines do not respond.

(iii) HOFFMANN BROMAMIDE DEGRADATION converts an amide to a primary amine with ONE CARBON FEWER:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The lost carbon is the CARBONYL carbon, leaving as carbonate, while the alkyl group migrates to the nitrogen.

rows.stem:
Write the structures of A, B and C in the following reactions :
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Cl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KCN}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow[0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}]{\mathrm{HNO_2}} \mathrm{C}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NH_3}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(b)\ H_2O}]{\mathrm{(a)\ LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}} \mathrm{C}\)
rows.solution:
(i) Potassium cyanide substitutes for the chloride, and the carbon count rises from two to three:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CN}\), propanenitrile

Lithium aluminium hydride reduces the nitrile all the way to a PRIMARY AMINE, with the carbon count unchanged:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\), propan-1-amine

Nitrous acid at \(0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) diazotises this ALIPHATIC amine, but the salt is unstable even at that temperature — it loses nitrogen at once and the cation picks up water:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\), propan-1-ol

(ii) Ammonia gives the ammonium salt, which loses water on heating to give the AMIDE:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}\), ethanamide

Lithium aluminium hydride reduces an amide to an amine with the carbon count UNCHANGED — note the contrast with Hofmann degradation, which would have lost a carbon:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\), ethanamine

Benzenesulphonyl chloride reacts with the primary amine's \(\mathrm{N-H}\) to give a sulphonamide:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2NHC_2H_5}\), N-ethylbenzenesulphonamide

This last is HINSBERG'S TEST. The product from a PRIMARY amine still has a hydrogen on the nitrogen, made acidic by the two sulphonyl oxygens, so it DISSOLVES in alkali — which is how a primary amine is told from a secondary one, whose sulphonamide has no such hydrogen and stays insoluble.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(i) Transition elements have higher enthalpies of atomisation.
(ii) Separation of a mixture of Lanthanoid elements is difficult.
(iii) The \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) value for copper is positive.
rows.solution:
(i) Because of STRONG METALLIC BONDING, arising from their UNPAIRED d ELECTRONS.

The enthalpy of atomisation measures the energy needed to pull an atom out of the metal, so it measures the strength of the bond holding the lattice together. In a transition metal the unpaired d electrons take part in that bonding ALONGSIDE the \(s\) electrons, so many more electrons are involved than in a main-group metal.

The trend within the series follows: the more unpaired d electrons, the stronger the bond. Chromium, with six, has one of the highest values; zinc, with none, has the lowest.

(ii) Because the lanthanoids are almost IDENTICAL IN SIZE and in chemical behaviour.

Across the series the \(4f\) electrons shield the nucleus poorly, so the steady rise in nuclear charge pulls the outer shells inwards — the LANTHANOID CONTRACTION. The ionic radii therefore fall only very slightly from one element to the next.

Since chemical properties depend largely on size and charge, and every one of them is predominantly \(+3\), their compounds behave alike — so they cannot be separated by ordinary chemical means, and ion-exchange or solvent extraction, exploiting minute differences, must be used instead.

(iii) Because copper has a HIGH enthalpy of atomisation and a LOW hydration enthalpy.

Converting the solid metal to hydrated \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) takes three steps, and the energy recovered in the last must pay for the first two. Pulling an atom out of the metal costs a great deal, removing two electrons costs more, and copper's hydration enthalpy does NOT cover both.

The process is therefore unfavourable and \(E^{\circ}\) comes out at \(+0{\cdot}34\) V — the only positive value in the 3d series, and the reason copper does not dissolve in hydrochloric or dilute sulphuric acid.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Define transition elements. Which of the d-block elements may not be regarded as the transition elements ? Why transition metals generally form coloured compounds ?
rows.solution:
A TRANSITION ELEMENT is one whose atom, or one of whose stable ions, has a PARTLY FILLED d SUBSHELL.

The two conditions matter equally. Copper is \(3d^{10}\) as the ATOM, which would seem to exclude it, but \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is \(3d^9\) — partly filled — so copper IS a transition element.

The d-block elements NOT regarded as transition elements are ZINC, CADMIUM and MERCURY, the group 12 metals.

They are \(d^{10}\) as atoms AND \(d^{10}\) as their \(+2\) ions, so neither condition is met. Everything that follows from a partly filled d subshell is absent from them: their compounds are white and diamagnetic, they show only the \(+2\) state, they are poor catalysts, and their melting points are unusually low.

TRANSITION METALS FORM COLOURED COMPOUNDS because of D-D TRANSITIONS. A ligand field splits the five d orbitals into two sets of different energy; an electron absorbs a photon of visible light and jumps from the lower set to the upper, and the colour seen is what remains of the white light after that absorption.

The jump needs BOTH an electron in the lower set and a vacancy in the upper — which is exactly why \(d^0\) ions such as \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) and \(d^{10}\) ions such as \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) are colourless, having no electron to promote or nowhere to promote it to.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
An organic compound 'X' with the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}O}\) forms 2,4-DNP derivative, does not reduce Tollens' reagent but gives positive iodoform test on heating with \(\mathrm{I_2}\) in the presence of NaOH. Compound 'X' gives ethanoic acid and propanoic acid on vigorous oxidation. Write the
(i) Structure of the compound 'X'.
(ii) Structure of the product obtained when compound 'X' reacts with 2,4-DNP reagent.
(iii) Structures of the products obtained when compound 'X' is heated with \(\mathrm{I_2}\) in the presence of NaOH.
rows.solution:
Take the four clues in turn, since each removes a possibility.

Forms a 2,4-DNP DERIVATIVE: the compound has a CARBONYL group.
Does NOT reduce TOLLENS' REAGENT: it is not an aldehyde, so it is a KETONE.
Positive IODOFORM TEST: it has a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group.
Vigorous oxidation gives ETHANOIC and PROPANOIC acids: the carbon chain is cut at the carbonyl, and the two fragments carry two and three carbons.

(i) The only structure satisfying all four is
\(\mathrm{X} = \mathrm{CH_3{-}CO{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CH_3}\), PENTAN-2-ONE

Cleaving on one side of the carbonyl gives the two-carbon acid, on the other the three-carbon acid, which is what vigorous oxidation reports.

(ii) 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water. The carbonyl oxygen is replaced by \(=\mathrm{N{-}NH{-}Ar}\):
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}C(CH_2CH_2CH_3){=}N{-}NH{-}C_6H_3(NO_2)_2}\)

The right-hand ring carries its two nitro groups at positions 2 and 4, counting from the carbon bearing the nitrogen. Such derivatives are orange-red crystalline solids with sharp melting points.

[The marking scheme's drawing of this product prints \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) in place of the second \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) on the ring; the reagent is drawn correctly, so it is a slip in the figure rather than a different product.]

(iii) The iodoform reaction attacks the \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group, replacing its three hydrogens by iodine and then cleaving the bond to the carbonyl. The CARBONYL CARBON stays with the larger fragment:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_2CH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{I_2}/\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CHI_3}\downarrow + \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2COONa}\)

The products are IODOFORM, a yellow precipitate, and SODIUM BUTANOATE.

rows.stem: Write any three differences between physisorption and chemisorption.
rows.solution:
Three differences between physisorption and chemisorption.

NATURE OF THE FORCES. PHYSISORPTION arises from weak VAN DER WAALS forces between the adsorbate and the surface. CHEMISORPTION involves genuine CHEMICAL BONDS, a compound effectively forming at the surface.

REVERSIBILITY. Physisorption is REVERSIBLE — the weak forces are easily overcome, so lowering the pressure or raising the temperature releases the gas. Chemisorption is essentially IRREVERSIBLE, the chemical bond being far harder to break.

NUMBER OF LAYERS. Physisorption forms MULTIMOLECULAR layers, since a physisorbed layer can attract further molecules on top of it. Chemisorption forms a UNIMOLECULAR layer only, because once every surface site has formed its bond there is nothing left to bond to.

Two further contrasts follow from the same difference in bond strength. The enthalpy of adsorption is small for physisorption, about 20 to 40 kJ per mole, and large for chemisorption, 80 to 240. And physisorption is NOT SPECIFIC — any gas will physisorb on any solid — whereas chemisorption is HIGHLY SPECIFIC, occurring only where a bond can actually form.

rows.stem:
Define the following terms with a suitable example in each :
(i) Lyophilic sol
(ii) Macromolecular colloid
(iii) Coagulation
rows.solution:
(i) A LYOPHILIC SOL is a colloid in which the particles of the DISPERSED PHASE have a strong AFFINITY for the dispersion medium — "solvent loving".

Such a sol forms simply on mixing the substance with the medium, needs no special method of preparation, and re-forms if the medium is evaporated and added back, so it is REVERSIBLE. It is also stable, the solvent layer around each particle protecting it.

EXAMPLE: gum in water; starch, gelatin and rubber in suitable media behave the same way.

(ii) A MACROMOLECULAR COLLOID is one obtained by dissolving substances whose MOLECULES are themselves large enough to fall in the colloidal range, \(1\) to \(1000\) nm.

Here the colloidal particle is a SINGLE MOLECULE rather than an aggregate of many, which is what distinguishes this class from associated colloids such as soap. These sols are generally lyophilic and stable.

EXAMPLE: starch in water; proteins, cellulose and synthetic polymers such as polythene and nylon give the same kind of sol.

(iii) COAGULATION is the settling of colloidal particles — the conversion of a colloidal sol into a PRECIPITATE.

It happens when the charge on the particles is neutralised, so that they can no longer repel one another, and they collide and grow heavy enough to fall out.

EXAMPLE: adding an electrolyte such as sodium chloride to a sol; electrophoresis, persistent dialysis, boiling and mixing two oppositely charged sols all do the same. The deposition of the Ganges delta, where river colloids meet sea water, is coagulation on a geographical scale.

rows.stem:
(a) The standard Gibbs energy \((\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}\mathrm{G}^{\circ})\) for the following cell reaction is \(-300\) kJ \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\) :
\(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}\,(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\)
Calculate \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}}\) for the reaction. (Given: 1F = 96500 \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
(b) Calculate \(\lambda^{o}_{m}\) for \(\mathrm{MgCl_2}\) if \(\lambda^{o}\) values for \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) ion and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ion are 106 S \(\mathrm{cm^2mol^{-1}}\) and 76.3 S \(\mathrm{cm^2mol^{-1}}\) respectively.
rows.solution:
(a) The standard free energy change and the cell potential are linked by
\(\Delta_r \mathrm{G}^{\circ} = -n\mathrm{F}E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}\)

The reaction \(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{Ag^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{Ag}\) transfers TWO electrons, so \(n = 2\). Converting the energy to joules:
\(-300 \times 10^{3} = -2 \times 96500 \times E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}\)
\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = \dfrac{300 \times 10^{3}}{2 \times 96500} = \dfrac{300000}{193000}\)

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 1{\cdot}55\ \mathrm{V}\)

The signs are the check: a NEGATIVE free energy change and a POSITIVE cell potential both mean the same thing, that the reaction is spontaneous.

(b) KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW adds the individual ionic contributions, each counted as often as the formula unit provides it. Magnesium chloride gives ONE magnesium ion and TWO chlorides:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}} + 2\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cl^-}}\)
\(= 106 + 2 \times 76{\cdot}3 = 106 + 152{\cdot}6\)

\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = 258{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The factor of 2 is what the question is testing. Forgetting it would give 182.3, and the error is invisible unless the formula is read carefully.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Arrange the following in the increasing order of their reactivity towards nucleophilic addition reaction. :
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), \(\mathrm{HCHO}\), \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}\)
rows.context:
Aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids are some of the important classes of organic compounds containing carbonyl group. These are highly polar molecules due to higher electro-negativity of oxygen relative to carbon in the carbonyl group. Aldehydes are prepared by dehydrogenation or controlled oxidation of primary alcohols and controlled reduction of acyl halides. Ketones are prepared by oxidation of secondary alcohols and hydration of alkynes.
Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition reactions onto the carbonyl group but carboxylic acid does not undergo nucleophilic addition reaction. The alpha \((\alpha)\) – hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones are acidic. Therefore aldehydes and ketones having at least one \(\alpha\)-hydrogen undergo Aldol condensation.
Aldehydes are easily oxidised by mild oxidising agents such as Tollens' reagent and Fehling's reagent. Carboxylic acids are prepared by the oxidation of primary alcohols, aldehydes and by hydrolysis of nitriles. Aromatic carboxylic acids are prepared by side-chain oxidation of alkyl benzenes. Carboxylic acids are considerably more acidic than alcohols and most of simple phenols.
rows.solution:
Increasing reactivity towards nucleophilic addition:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3CHO} < \mathrm{HCHO}\)

Nucleophilic addition begins with a nucleophile attacking the carbonyl carbon, so reactivity falls as that carbon is made less positive and more crowded — and both ALKYL and ARYL groups do this.

Count the substituents. Methanal has NO alkyl group on the carbonyl carbon, ethanal has ONE, propanone has TWO — so the reactivity falls in that order, each group releasing electron density inductively and blocking the approach.

Acetophenone is the least reactive of all. Its PHENYL group withdraws inductively but, far more importantly, DELOCALISES the carbonyl \(\pi\) system into the ring by resonance, relieving the carbon of positive charge; and the flat ring is bulkier than a methyl group.

Methanal is so reactive on this count that in water it exists largely as its hydrate.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Give a simple chemical test to distinguish between Ethanal and Propanone.
rows.context:
Aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids are some of the important classes of organic compounds containing carbonyl group. These are highly polar molecules due to higher electro-negativity of oxygen relative to carbon in the carbonyl group. Aldehydes are prepared by dehydrogenation or controlled oxidation of primary alcohols and controlled reduction of acyl halides. Ketones are prepared by oxidation of secondary alcohols and hydration of alkynes.
Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition reactions onto the carbonyl group but carboxylic acid does not undergo nucleophilic addition reaction. The alpha \((\alpha)\) – hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones are acidic. Therefore aldehydes and ketones having at least one \(\alpha\)-hydrogen undergo Aldol condensation.
Aldehydes are easily oxidised by mild oxidising agents such as Tollens' reagent and Fehling's reagent. Carboxylic acids are prepared by the oxidation of primary alcohols, aldehydes and by hydrolysis of nitriles. Aromatic carboxylic acids are prepared by side-chain oxidation of alkyl benzenes. Carboxylic acids are considerably more acidic than alcohols and most of simple phenols.
rows.solution:
Use TOLLENS' REAGENT, an ammoniacal solution of silver nitrate. Warmed with ETHANAL it gives a bright SILVER MIRROR on the inside of the tube, the aldehyde being oxidised to ethanoic acid while silver ion is reduced to the metal. PROPANONE gives no reaction, a ketone resisting such mild oxidation.

Fehling's solution serves the same way: ethanal gives a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, propanone gives none.

Note which test would FAIL here. Both compounds contain a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group, so BOTH give a positive IODOFORM test — it cannot distinguish them. The distinction has to rest on the aldehyde's ease of oxidation, which is the one property the ketone does not share.

rows.subtopic: Nomenclature and Structure of Carboxyl Group
rows.stem: Why carboxylic acid does not give nucleophilic addition reactions like aldehydes and ketones ?
rows.context:
Aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids are some of the important classes of organic compounds containing carbonyl group. These are highly polar molecules due to higher electro-negativity of oxygen relative to carbon in the carbonyl group. Aldehydes are prepared by dehydrogenation or controlled oxidation of primary alcohols and controlled reduction of acyl halides. Ketones are prepared by oxidation of secondary alcohols and hydration of alkynes.
Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition reactions onto the carbonyl group but carboxylic acid does not undergo nucleophilic addition reaction. The alpha \((\alpha)\) – hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones are acidic. Therefore aldehydes and ketones having at least one \(\alpha\)-hydrogen undergo Aldol condensation.
Aldehydes are easily oxidised by mild oxidising agents such as Tollens' reagent and Fehling's reagent. Carboxylic acids are prepared by the oxidation of primary alcohols, aldehydes and by hydrolysis of nitriles. Aromatic carboxylic acids are prepared by side-chain oxidation of alkyl benzenes. Carboxylic acids are considerably more acidic than alcohols and most of simple phenols.
rows.solution:
Because the carboxyl carbon is stabilised by RESONANCE with the hydroxyl oxygen.

In a carboxylic acid the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) oxygen donates a lone pair into the carbonyl group, so resonance structures can be drawn placing a negative charge on the carbonyl oxygen and a positive one on the hydroxyl oxygen — with the carbon between them relieved of much of its deficiency.

That carbon therefore carries far LESS positive charge than a plain carbonyl carbon does, and in effect loses its carbonyl character. A nucleophile finds little to attack.

An aldehyde or ketone has no such donor beside the carbonyl — only hydrogen or alkyl groups, which cannot supply a lone pair — so its carbon stays strongly electrophilic.

The consequence is that carboxylic acids do NOT give the characteristic additions of the carbonyl group: no bisulphite addition, no cyanohydrin, no condensation with ammonia derivatives.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Why \(\alpha\)-hydrogen of aldehydes and ketones are acidic in nature ?
(ii) Write the products in the following :
\(2\,\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Conc} \cdot \mathrm{NaOH}}\)

rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — Sub-part (ii)'s reactant is DRAWN: a hexagonal benzene ring bonded to —CHO, with the stoichiometric coefficient 2 in front, above a reaction arrow labelled 'Conc . NaOH'. The formula above is a faithful naming of that drawing, not an approximation, but the page shows a structure, so the real crop should be attached. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(i) Because the CARBANION left behind is stabilised by RESONANCE with the carbonyl group.

Removing an \(\alpha\) hydrogen leaves a negative charge on the carbon next to the carbonyl, and that charge does not stay there — it is delocalised onto the OXYGEN, which is far better able to carry it, being the more electronegative atom:
\(\mathrm{{}^-CH_2{-}CH{=}O} \longleftrightarrow \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}O^-}\)

The resulting ENOLATE is stable enough for a base to remove the hydrogen, which it could never do from an ordinary alkane. This acidity is what makes the aldol condensation and \(\alpha\)-halogenation possible.

(ii) Benzaldehyde has NO \(\alpha\) HYDROGEN — the only carbon beside its carbonyl is part of the ring — so it cannot undergo aldol condensation. With concentrated alkali it undergoes CANNIZZARO'S REACTION instead, a disproportionation in which one molecule is oxidised and another reduced:
\(2\,\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2OH} + \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa}\)

The products are BENZYL ALCOHOL and SODIUM BENZOATE, the free acid being obtained on acidification.

rows.stem:
Write the major products of the following reactions :
(i) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2-CH_3} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(b)\ H^{+}}]{\mathrm{(a)\ KMnO_4,\ KOH}}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2,\ Pd\text{-}BaSO_4}}\)

The formulae above name those drawings faithfully rather than approximating them, but the page shows structures, so the real crops should be attached. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(i) Alkaline permanganate oxidises the whole side chain back to a single carboxyl carbon, and acidification frees the acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2CH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{KMnO_4}/\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOK} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

The product is BENZOIC ACID. The second carbon of the ethyl group is lost entirely — the oxidation attacks the BENZYLIC carbon and cuts the chain there, so toluene and ethylbenzene give the same product.

(ii) Hydrogen over palladium supported on barium sulphate is ROSENMUND'S REDUCTION, which converts an acyl chloride to an ALDEHYDE:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow[\text{barium sulphate}]{\mathrm{Pd}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The product is BENZALDEHYDE. The catalyst is deliberately POISONED — with sulphur or quinoline, and by the inert barium sulphate support — so that it is not active enough to reduce the aldehyde further to benzyl alcohol. Controlling the catalyst is the whole point of the method.
